name: Manumanaw Karen
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Wai Lin Aung 2013, A descriptive grammar of Kayah Monu (Payap Univ. MA thesis); also Myar Doo Myar Reh 2004, A phonological comparison of selected Karenic language varieties of Kayah State

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2021. Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Sidwell & Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, ch. 18. De Gruyter.
sources.note: General only: 'Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words' (unstressed atonal minor syllable + stressed full syllable, exemplified for Pwo, Sgaw, Kayah Li, Kayan, Geba); cites Wai Lin Aung 2013 only for Manu orthography (p.14) and negation type. No Manu-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2009. Prolegomena to reconstructing Proto-Karen. La Trobe Papers in Linguistics 12.
sources.note: Manu appears as a wordlist column and in the classification (Manu-Kayaw cluster); the only stress remark is areal ('Most languages of Southeast Asia are sesquisyllabic (i.e. they have iambic stress)'), not about Manu.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record manu1255 (Kayaw-Manu < Central Karen < Karenic).
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Wai Lin Aung 2013, Myar 2004.

sources.citation: Myar Doo Myar Reh. 2004. A phonological comparison of selected Karenic language varieties of Kayah State. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xix+180 pp. (Monumanaw = Monu dialect of Dolaso, Phruso township).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Sec. 3.3 Monumanaw (pp. 90-109): syllable types CVT and CCVT, 22 consonants, 14 clusters, 10 vowels, four contrastive tones (high, high-mid, mid, low); p. 108: in three-syllable words 'There are no examples of M or HM occurring on the first or second syllable... strong tendency for them to also not occur on the final syllable' (tone distribution, not a stress statement). Ch. 4 p. 136: template C1(C2)V T, open syllables only.

sources.citation: Wai Lin Aung. 2013. A descriptive grammar of Kayah Monu. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xiv+194 pp. (PDF 210 pp.; Taw Khu dialect). fetched sources from the Google Drive link cited in en.wikipedia 'Karenni language' (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dkC3Mcfjgt7N7_kliLgd2TaTOp5PjwSJ/view); Payap upload URL now 404.
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 1.8 'Brief Phonology of Kayah Monu' (pp. 11-14, PDF pp. 27-30) gives 22 consonants, 10 vowels, four contrastive tones (footnote: researcher hypothesises only three level tones), open syllables only, 'template for main syllable structure is C1(C2)V'; phonology explicitly taken from Myar 2004. grep stress/accent/unstressed/sesquisyllabic/minor syllable/iambic/prominence: no hits (only dialect 'accent'). Affixation section (2.4.2, prefixes ta-, ʔə-) says nothing prosodic.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2011. The subgrouping of Karen. SEALS 21 paper + handouts.
sources.note: Manu data columns (rhyme reflexes), Kayaw-Manu cluster; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kauffman, William G. 1993. The great tone split and Central Karen. MA thesis, University of North Dakota.

sources.note: Phoneme tables for Western Kayah citing Bryant 1996 and Wai Lin Aung 2013; orthography marks tones and breathy voice; nothing on stress. Supplied the open Google Drive link to the 2013 thesis.
